title: Re-theorising mobility and the formation of culture and language among the Corded Ware Culture in Europe
authors: Kristiansen K., Allentoft M.E., Frei K.M., Iversen R., Johannsen N.N., Kroonen G., Pospieszny Ł., Price T.D., Rasmussen S., Sjögren K.-G., et al.
ask_addressed: What does ancient DNA, archaeology and historical linguistics show about the spread of Indo-European languages (steppe/Yamnaya hypothesis, Anatolian hypothesis, Indo-Iranian branch)? Dates, routes, and the strength of each hypothesis.
quote: we are finally in a position where migrations can be documented rather than debated as an element in the formation of the Corded Ware Culture
summary: Summarises aDNA (Allentoft 2015, Haak 2015) showing extensive gene flow into temperate Europe shortly after 3000 BC, and explains Corded Ware as hybridisation of migrant Yamnaya people with local Neolithic groups, with isotope evidence for exogamy.
limits: A synthesis by authors who are themselves proponents (several co-authored the Nature papers); the people movement is what is documented, the language shift is an inference. Open access (CC BY).

title: Re-theorising mobility and the formation of culture and language among the Corded Ware Culture in Europe
authors: Kristiansen K., Allentoft M.E., Frei K.M., Iversen R., Johannsen N.N., Kroonen G., Pospieszny Ł., Price T.D., Rasmussen S., Sjögren K.-G., et al.
ask_addressed: What does ancient DNA, archaeology and historical linguistics show about the spread of Indo-European languages (steppe/Yamnaya hypothesis, Anatolian hypothesis, Indo-Iranian branch)? Dates, routes, and the strength of each hypothesis.
quote: The result of this hybridisation process was the formation of a new material culture, the Corded Ware Culture, and of a new dialect, Proto-Germanic.
summary: Argues from the same genetic, isotopic and linguistic data that the migrant steppe population carried an Indo-European dialect, which hybridised with local speech to give Proto-Germanic (new crop words adopted).
limits: The linking of the migrant population to a specific language and dialect rests on linguistic reasoning and the Yamnaya=PIE identification, not on any text or inscription.

title: Discussion: Are the Origins of Indo-European Languages Explained by the Migration of the Yamnaya Culture to the West?
authors: Klejn L.S., Haak W., Lazaridis I., Patterson N., Reich D., Kristiansen K., Sjögren K.-G., Allentoft M., Sikora M., Willerslev E.
venue: European Journal of Archaeology (published online 28 July 2017)
ask_addressed: What are the principal sceptical or alternative views, and what remains unresolved?
quote: Klejn, however, has come to the conclusion that the authors' objections do not assuage his doubts.
summary: Abstract of a published exchange: Klejn criticises the genetic inference and its use for the Indo-European question; the Nature authors reply; Klejn rejects the replies.
limits: Only the abstract is open (full text behind 'Get access'); the specific arguments of either side were not read. The volume/issue was not shown in the page text read, so the venue is given as the journal only.

title: Massive Migrations? The Impact of Recent aDNA Studies on our View of Third Millennium Europe
venue: European Journal of Archaeology (published online 28 Sep 2017)
ask_addressed: What are the principal sceptical or alternative views, and what remains unresolved?
quote: Since the new aDNA data are used to create vivid narratives describing 'massive migrations', the so-called cultural groups are once again likened to human populations
summary: Archaeological critique: aDNA findings on Yamnaya, Corded Ware and Bell Beaker are narrated in a culture-historical way that treats archaeological cultures as bounded populations; calls for anthropological migration models. Accepts the new data, disputes the 'massive migration' framing.
limits: Critiques interpretation, not the genetic measurements. The paper states it is not the place to discuss the Indo-European issue, so it bears on the language question only indirectly.

title: Prehistory by Bayesian phylogenetics? The state of the art on Indo-European origins
ask_addressed: What are the principal sceptical or alternative views, and what remains unresolved?
quote: in the Indo-European case the results from Bayesian phylogenetics continue to reinforce the argument for an Anatolian rather than a Steppe origin
summary: Review of Bayesian phylogenetic dating studies (Gray, Atkinson, Bouckaert and others): Heggarty finds them increasingly sophisticated, names remaining concerns, and still reads the Indo-European results as favouring an Anatolian origin.
limits: Abstract only (full text behind access). 2014, so before the 2015 aDNA papers. The lexical-dating results are model-dependent and the author lists remaining concerns.

title: Twenty-first-century light over the Indo-European homeland: triangulating language, archaeology and genetics
ask_addressed: What are the principal sceptical or alternative views, and what remains unresolved?
quote: this has not yet been settled and other routes remain possible
summary: A 2024 review states that the Anatolian branch is the earliest split on the family tree and that whether the Anatolian languages entered from the west (via the Balkans) or by another route is unsettled, while the Yamnaya-Corded Ware-Sintashta-Indo-Iranic line fits the Indo-European dispersal.
limits: Review of a book, not original research. Open access (CC BY).

title: Indo-European loanwords and exchange in Bronze Age Central and East Asia
ask_addressed: What does ancient DNA, archaeology and historical linguistics show about the spread of Indo-European languages (steppe/Yamnaya hypothesis, Anatolian hypothesis, Indo-Iranian branch)? Dates, routes, and the strength of each hypothesis.
quote: the six items can be dated to have entered Central and East Asian languages from immigrant Indo-European languages spoken in the Afanasievo and Andronovo cultures
summary: Comparative-method analysis of six loanwords shared between Indo-European, Uralic, Turkic and Old Chinese, dated to Bronze Age contact with Afanasievo and Andronovo Indo-European speakers.
limits: Concerns eastward Indo-European speakers (Afanasievo, Andronovo) and does not itself test the Indo-Iranian route into Iran or India. Loanword dating is argued, not independently dated. Open access (CC BY).

title: Beyond binaries. Interrogating ancient DNA
ask_addressed: What are the principal sceptical or alternative views, and what remains unresolved?
quote: We suggest that at present much aDNA research rests upon two problematic theoretical assumptions
summary: A general critique of aDNA archaeology: nature/culture binary and treating cultures as bounded identities. Not specific to Indo-European, but it is the theoretical basis for much of the sceptical reading of steppe-migration narratives.
limits: Abstract only; general to aDNA, not about Indo-European specifically. Authors and year were not read from the page, so they are left unrecorded.
